content.text: {"primary_meaning": "Sodom and Gomorrah function as the Bible's paradigmatic symbol of extreme human wickedness and of sudden, total divine judgment. Across Christian teaching the cities serve as the proverbial example of what happens when sin reaches full measure: complete, irreversible destruction from God. They are invoked as a warning-type — a byword for depravity and a standing image of eschatological judgment — such that to compare a people or city to Sodom is to declare it ripe for condemnation.", "primary_basis": ["Genesis 13:13", "Genesis 18:20-33", "Genesis 19:1-29", "Deuteronomy 29:23", "Isaiah 1:9-10", "Isaiah 13:19", "Jeremiah 23:14", "Jeremiah 49:18", "Lamentations 4:6", "Amos 4:11", "Zephaniah 2:9", "Matthew 10:15", "Matthew 11:23-24", "Luke 17:28-32", "Romans 9:29", "2 Peter 2:6-9", "Jude 7", "Revelation 11:8"], "alternatives": [{"meaning": "A symbol specifically of sexual immorality, and in much traditional teaching specifically of homosexual acts ('sodomy'). This reading takes the demand of the men of Sodom in Genesis 19:4-5 and the phrase 'sexual immorality and unnatural desire' in Jude 7 as identifying the defining sin of the cities.", "basis": ["Genesis 19:4-11", "Jude 7", "2 Peter 2:6-10"], "prominence": "common"}, {"meaning": "A symbol of pride, luxury, injustice, and failure to care for the poor and needy — based on Ezekiel's explicit indictment. This reading, prominent in modern scholarship and in Jewish tradition, treats social sin rather than sexual sin as the core of Sodom's guilt.", "basis": ["Ezekiel 16:49-50", "Isaiah 1:10-17", "Jeremiah 23:14"], "prominence": "common"}, {"meaning": "A symbol of the violation of hospitality: the attempted assault on Lot's guests represents the ultimate breach of ancient Near Eastern hospitality codes, contrasted with Abraham's and Lot's welcome of the visitors. Jesus' pairing of Sodom's fate with towns that refuse to receive his messengers is cited in support. Common among academic interpreters, minority in popular teaching.", "basis": ["Genesis 18:1-8", "Genesis 19:1-3", "Matthew 10:14-15", "Luke 10:10-12"], "prominence": "minority"}, {"meaning": "A typological symbol for apostate or corrupt cities of God's own people — especially Jerusalem — showing that covenant communities can become 'Sodom' when unfaithful. Prophets call Judah's rulers 'rulers of Sodom,' and Revelation names the city where the Lord was crucified 'Sodom and Egypt.'", "basis": ["Isaiah 1:9-10", "Isaiah 3:9", "Jeremiah 23:14", "Ezekiel 16:46-52", "Revelation 11:8"], "prominence": "minority"}, {"meaning": "An eschatological type of the suddenness and unexpectedness of final judgment, with 'remember Lot's wife' as a warning against looking back or clinging to a doomed world. This emphasizes not the nature of Sodom's sin but the abruptness of its end as a picture of the day of the Son of Man.", "basis": ["Luke 17:28-33", "Genesis 19:17-26", "2 Peter 2:6-9"], "prominence": "common"}], "has_settled_consensus": true, "confidence": "high", "notes": "There is broad, recognizable consensus that Sodom and Gomorrah symbolize consummate wickedness and total divine judgment — the cities are used this way as a stock byword throughout both Testaments and virtually all Christian traditions. What is genuinely contested is the identification of the specific sin that made them emblematic: traditional teaching (especially patristic through early modern) foregrounded sexual sin, particularly homosexual acts, while much modern scholarship and some ecclesial traditions foreground pride, injustice, and inhospitality per Ezekiel 16:49. These strands are not mutually exclusive and are often combined (Ezekiel 16:50's 'abomination' is read variously). The dispute over the sin does not undermine the settled consensus on the symbolic function: exemplary judgment on grave sin."}
